title: Oil Paint and the North
objective: After this level you can explain how Flemish painters like van Eyck used oil paint for fine detail.
summary: Egg tempera dries fast; oil dries slowly, so tones blend in thin glazes. Jan van Eyck perfected oil in Bruges, and his 1434 Arnolfini Portrait shows a whole room in a mirror.

cards.headline: A painting from 1434 has writing on its wall: "Jan van Eyck was here."
cards.body: It's in Latin, in curly script, right above a mirror in the Arnolfini Portrait: Johannes de Eyck fuit hic. 1434. To see why people marveled at this painter, you need to know what was in his paint.

items.label: Egg tempera
points: Dries fast, so tones can't blend

items.label: Oil paint
points: Pigment in a drying oil, like linseed
Dries slowly, so tones can blend
Laid on in thin, see-through glazes

mascot.line: Egg or oil? The quick test is blending. Egg dries too fast; oil dries slowly, so tones can blend.

cards.headline: A whole room in a mirror
cards.body: Van Eyck didn't invent oil painting, but he perfected it, building pictures from thin, transparent glazes. In the Arnolfini Portrait a richly dressed man and woman, probably the Italian merchant Giovanni Arnolfini and his wife, stand in a room in Bruges with a red bed and a brass chandelier. The round, convex mirror on the back wall shows the room again: the couple from behind, and two men coming in at the door. Is one of them the painter? Scholars still debate it.

cards.fact: An Italian said his paintings looked made by nature, not by hands.
cards.context: That was in 1449, from an Italian humanist. Oil soon won over the south: in 16th-century Venice it became painters' basic material. And remember Leonardo's sfumato from Level 35? Those thin, melting layers were possible because oil paint was still fairly new in Italy.

cards.headline: Oil: mastered
learned: Tempera dries fast; oil dries slowly and blends
Van Eyck perfected oil with thin glazes
The Arnolfini mirror reflects the whole room

questions.prompt: Why could oil painters blend tones smoothly when tempera painters crosshatched?

options.label: Tempera has no pigment in it
options.rationale: Both use pigment; the binder differs.

options.label: Oil dries slowly, so tones can blend
Tempera is always painted on walls

questions.explanation: Egg tempera dries fast, so painters shaded with crosshatching. Oil dries slowly, so tones can be blended.

questions.prompt: Leonardo's sfumato melts light into dark in thin layers. What made that possible?

options.label: Egg tempera
options.rationale: Tempera dries too fast to blend.

options.rationale: Prints don't give you soft painted shading.

Fresco on wet plaster
